concept.name: Zero-coupon bond
concept.definition: A bond that pays no periodic interest; it is issued or created at a deep discount to face value, and the investor's entire return comes from accretion to the full face value at maturity. U.S. Treasury STRIPS create zero-coupon securities by separately trading the individual interest and principal components of Treasury notes, bonds, and TIPS.
concept.intuition: A zero-coupon bond bundles all its interest into the purchase discount: you pay a fraction of face value today and receive one certain payment on one known future date.
concept.mechanics: The price is the present value of face value at the bond's yield, and the implied interest compounds internally until maturity. With all cash flow at maturity, a zero's duration equals its maturity, making it highly sensitive to rate changes; in taxable accounts, the accrued interest is generally taxable annually even though nothing is paid out ('phantom income').
concept.formula: Price = F / (1 + y)^T, where F is face value, y the yield per period, and T the number of periods.
concept.failure_modes: Zeros carry the maximum duration for their maturity, so rising rates produce outsized price losses. Phantom-income taxation creates cash-flow drag, and corporate zeros add credit risk on a single distant payment.
concept.misconceptions: That no coupon means no interest — the discount embodies the full interest. Also, while zeros have no reinvestment risk, they are not low-risk: their price volatility is higher than any coupon bond of the same maturity.
concept.example: A 10-year zero-coupon bond yielding 5% costs about $613.91 per $1,000 face value and pays exactly $1,000 at maturity.
